music here is pretty dang good, reminds me a lot of the trance music from the days of half life 2

but in another way, gordon freeman strangely felt more respected in the first game, having to oversee their finest sample yet, and then do everything to save the situation, kind of like doug rattman sneaking around the facility
but in this game the relationship is much more indirect, where people speak about things that surround you rather than what you really do, even barney kind of understands you as a great figure,
though those more formal parts still exist among certain voice lines, particularly from the vortegaunts

episode 1

A game attains legendary status for a reason. What do I even say.. After hearing about this game for so many years, I finally sat down to play it and my god does it live up to the hype.

For those of you who are curious, I highly recommend playing half life 1 prior to this, because it is a continuation of the story and several times throughout the game the character will refer back to scenarios that happened in the first game. I'm coming into this iteration after having finished HL1, so do with that info what you may.


GAMEPLAY:
It takes all the good things learnt from HL1 and improves on it. The addition of the trusty gravity gun also gives the entire game a new angle, one where you have to modify the environment around you to fit your needs, or at the very least you can use it in combat by yeeting things at any enemies.
There were several times where it changed into a horror game, with you having to conserve ammunition and take your shots carefully so as to not waste bullets. It was a surprising change, but not necessarily a bad one. The game also constantly changed pace, going from combat to puzzles to story so it never got dry. All in all, I never felt bored during my playtime, no matter what I was doing. That should be enough to convince you they've done well.

STORY:
Half life ends on a note that makes you want more... I was always curious about why HL3 was spoken about, and eagerly anticipated. After that ending... I get it. There is nothing more that needs to be said.


I would write a longer review, but that would be me rambling about a game that I believe speaks for itself.

Play Half Life 1, and then play Half Life 2. Do not skip out on either of them.

Half-Life 2 picks up just about where we left off in the first Half-Life which allows the developers to expand this wonderful and terrifying sci-fi world. In addition to continued world-building, this sequel showcases technological and graphical upgrades across the board. And, a greater emphasis on dialogue and the development of a small cast of characters promises a more tangible story that was lacking in the original. While the Source Engine--beloved by all in Garry's Mod--truly revolutionizes the Half-Life gameplay formula, the promise of a more substantive narrative disappointingly goes unfulfilled. 

Like the original, this game is an extremely linear FPS that keeps the player engaged through varied environments, an ever-expanding arsenal of guns, and core combat mechanics that build on themselves in satisfying progressions. However, Half-Life 2 has so much more to offer. I do love the aesthetics and charm of the original, but the sequel is stunning. The player spends so much more time above ground, and, combined with a couple of vehicle levels, there are so many beautiful environments to take in. More open spaces also help the developers explore new emotional tones. When I think of the first Half-Life I think of anxiety--knowing that danger was around every corner and feeling like my back was always against the wall. Half-Life 2 certainly has these moments, but it's refreshing to see them blended with levels that are calmer, levels that are somewhat triumphant, and levels/moments of genuine horror. While the first game was creepy and stressful, it never made me jump out of my seat in fear like this game did on more than one occassion. Another massive improvement is the platforming, as in, this game doesn't really have any. Easily the weakest part of the first game, I'm happy to see its presence greatly reduced. I don't regret playing the first, but Half-Life 2 does laps around its predecessor regarding its robust and inspired gameplay. 

Where these games are more comparable is in their story-telling. The original Half-Life is presented almost as a mystery that is told largely through the environments themselves. By the end of the game, the player has a loose grasp on what is actually going on and ends up with more questions than answers. With more dialogue, more time for character moments, and a fully-fledged dystopian setting, I assumed Half-Life 2 was going to have more story. It doesn't, and it doesn't care to answer any of the questions raised in the first game either. I haven't yet played Episodes One and Two, so I'll update my review if necessary, but I'm disappointed at yet another barebones narrative. 

In spite of an underwhelming climax, Half-Life 2 consistently exceeded my expectations. I loved the visuals and atmosphere, and enjoyed the constant sense of adventure. The gameplay is robust: everything just works and I never needed a guide to help me progress. This game is a ton of fun and I'm already reminiscing on its many moments of "woah," "wow," and "what!?" This game deserves its reputation as a classic and, therefore, I strongly recommend Half-Life 2.

[h1]A defining series of games.[/h1]
I think its no secret that the Half-life games (From the first to Alyx) have had quite an impact on the industry, and for good reason, it made leaps in the industry that other companies adopted:
[list]
[*]Half-Life was one of the major games known for making an actual story and not just "run and shoot" simulators for shooters where the story is hidden away in the games manual.
[*] Half-Life 2 showed off insane physics engines and intractability that [i]personally I just don't really see replicated to this day,[/i] there's a reason Garry's Mod is still so damn popular even today.
[*] Half-life: Alyx helped make a big push for VR-story driven games, and even made it as accessible as possible for people who have different playstyles for VR (Obviously this is [i]less relevant for a review about Half-Life 2 and its episodes, but I felt it worth adding on).[/i]
[/list]

My point with this being that the games themselves are not just good because "waow valve OwO <3", its because they pushed the limits [i]at the time,[/i] they said to the world that "Hey, this is possible, you should do this". [b]Maybe compared to today these games don't hold up as well[/b] and that's okay frankly, these games were built for a different era.

[h3]But [u]why[/u] should I play it?[/h3]

Besides the aforementioned technological processes these games present; They do have a simple and compelling story, you don't need to remember a ton of tiny details. Obviously I'm writing this from the perspective of one who has hopefully played the first Half-Life game (But its also not mandatory), Half-Life does a lot of environmental storytelling, games these days will happily flash UI's in your screen or give you on-screen arrows and guides for what to do next; Half-Life doesn't do that, at most you will be given a brief flash on the side on how to do something (Like you pick up a new weapon with a secondary function? It tells you how to use it).

Valve has put a lot of effort into "Show, don't tell", they expect you to play around, to try something until that little gear clicks and you go "Oh hang on! I can do something here", from simple physics puzzles, different ways of approaching firefights, and generally dealing with different situations. The old motto of

[b]Run.[/b]
[b]Think.[/b]
[b]Shoot.[/b]
[b]Live.[/b]

Still really applies to the 2nd instalment of the series (I don't think it applies [i]as much[/i] to the episodic games).

Other points I'll quickly touch on:

[h3]Music[/h3]
The music to this game simply [b]hits.[/b] I confess there are a couple that make me go "eh." but a [i]large majority[/i] of the songs fit the moments, [i]especially[/i] in combat.

[h3]AI[/h3]
The AI here is quite well made, its one of those things where its [b]super[/b] easy to miss, because it works so well that it feels very fluid. If you have already played it or you're more interested in watching the game you can watch [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2M18hLbyKFo&list=PL9ANjLBdE91556Ik-5NRG11oPoB5uPbz3]videos of the AI in action[/url] and really appreciate the work that went into this for a [b]2004 game.[/b] It really forces you to think more about battles and combat (Especially on hard difficulty, which makes them stronger and you weaker as a challenge).

[h3]Generic NPC's[/h3]
I don't know how they do it, but somehow every NPC I've seen never feels like "Wow I've seen this exact face 50 times, how lazy", despite there only being a small handful of unique faces and even fewer voice lines, it somehow still keeps me engrossed in the story. This does have the rather unfortunate side effect of looking a bit too bland compared to the main characters.

[h2]Not all is perfect[/h2]
I recommend the game, flaws and all.

But, its not perfect, obviously 22 years have passed, [i]that's a long time for things to happen, be noticed, and for things that were once "fun, quirky" to be "annoying, boring" pretty quickly.[/i] This is really more of an issue after a first playthrough (As the series [i]does lack a bit of replayability)[/i] and when you start looking at how modern games have iterated on the model that Half-Life implemented.

There are issues with the game for sure though, examples being:
[list]
[*] One chapter partway through Half-Life 2 is just simply boring ([spoiler]Black Mesa East[/spoiler])
[*] Other chapters can feel very long and tedious, like they're overstaying their welcome ([spoiler]Water Hazard, Highway 17[/spoiler]), especially in some of these sections where the flow is constantly interrupted ([spoiler]Specifically Highway 17 and the Scout Car[/spoiler])
[*] Weapons can feel pretty weak at times, I played on hard (where your weapons do less damage) but it felt like I was having to dump entire magazines sometimes to kill an enemy, even with a shotgun at close range trying to go for headshots. It feels as if a large emphasis was placed on a particular physics based weapon ([spoiler]Gravity Gun[/spoiler]), on a related note, some weapons are very quickly overshadowed later on like the pistol where its use cases are more rare or for emergencies.
[*] On the topic of damage numbers, the difficulty selections are rather bland: Easy makes enemies weaker and your bullets deal more damage, Normal makes your bullets and theirs the same whilst being equal in armour/health, Hard makes you weaker and their damage hurt more. It just feels lazy that they don't do anything different.
[*] Episode 1 feels rather short in general (And I think is the weakest overall), and it doesn't really do anything that interesting outside of a couple sequences)
[*] Episode 2 has [b]very[/b] annoying achievements that require more patience than they're frankly worth ([spoiler]Little Rocket Man, Pinata Party[/spoiler])
[/list]

These are some gripes I've had, and others will certainly share.

But, despite these flaws, I think Half-Life 2 and its episodes are still games [i]worth trying out[/i] simply to get an idea of what it was accomplishing in [b]2004.[/b] Again, Valve was trying to push the bar with these games, [b]and its okay if people don't like it[/b], after all this is an old game (As much as I hate saying it, but 22 years is pretty long!), we've had a chance to learn from these games and improve on them, but sometimes its nice to play a classic.

Coming back to Half-Life 2 after all these years, it's every bit as fun as I remembered. The world feels alive, the characters are memorable, and every chapter leaves you wanting to see what happens next.
The combat is a blast. Fights stay fresh because the game keeps changing how you approach them, and the pacing between action, exploration, and quieter moments is spot on. Progression is super interesting too, always giving you something new so it never feels repetitive.
The graphics still look remarkable. Even after all this time, the art direction and atmosphere hold up better than a lot of modern games, and the whole thing feels polished.
Now a little rant: with all three games' achievements combined into one list, going for 100% is a bit hard. There's a lot to track, and some of them take real patience. But that's part of what makes it rewarding. It's challenging, yet still really enjoyable the whole way through.
Whether it's your first time or you're coming back for a replay, this one is worth your time. It's a classic for a reason. Highly recommend. A must play.
